corrected_value.title: A genome-wide association study for myopia and refractive error identifies a susceptibility locus at 15q25.

decisions.location: Introduction, paragraph 2; Methods and Results (15q25 results); Reference 14
decisions.quote: Two recent genome-wide association studies (GWASs) identified strong association with refractive error in two locations on chromosome 15. Solouki et al. [ 11 ] reported an association on 15q14 that was subsequently replicated in several other populations [ 12 , 13 ]. Hysi et al. [ 14 ] published a second locus on 15q25 at the same time.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent (never previously adjudicated). The primary full text empirically retests two distinct published chromosome 15 refractive-error GWAS discovery findings in the AREDS cohort (n=1,877/1,879): the 15q14 association of Solouki et al. (2010, reference [11], doi:10.1038/ng.663) and the 15q25 association of Hysi et al. (2010, reference [14], doi:10.1038/ng.664). For 15q25, the authors use Hysi et al.'s reported effect sizes (beta=-0.35, OR=1.16) for power calculations, test the 15q25 discovery SNP rs8027411, the CREAM replication SNPs, custom TaqMan tagging SNPs, and 1,224 array SNPs within 350 kb of rs8027411 against quantitative spherical equivalent, myopia, and hyperopia, and compare the non-replication of the original SNPs with significant regional association for hyperopia at rs7164400 (p=8.39x10^-4). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 2530, doi:10.1038/ng.663) represents only the companion Solouki et al. (2010) 15q14 discovery study (also coded as sibling target_index 0). Report equivalence does not apply because Hysi et al. (2010, Nat Genet 42:902-905) and Solouki et al. (2010, Nat Genet 42:897-901) are separate GWAS articles discovering different chromosomal loci (15q25 vs. 15q14) with different lead variants and discovery cohorts. Note that the intervening CREAM meta-analysis (Verhoeven et al., 2012, reference [15]) already included the AREDS cohort and is used here only for SNP selection context rather than as an independent target.

decisions.quote: The On Track program, previously found to be effective in a researcher-driven and tightly controlled setting, was implemented in a larger sample of schools. To investigate the robustness of the original findings, specific aspects of the implementation were deliberately altered from the original study.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent (never previously adjudicated). The supplied source text is an abstract-only record (with no in-text citation or reference list) that explicitly reports a conceptual replication of a single prior study evaluating the 'On Track' early reading intervention in a researcher-driven setting and compares its effect sizes to that original try-out. The blind coder recorded this single target with empty bibliographic fields because the abstract omits the citation. Shipped row 1566 (Solheim, Frijters, Lundetrae, & Uppstad, 2018, 'Effectiveness of an early reading intervention in a semi-transparent orthography: A group randomised controlled trial', Learning and Instruction, doi:10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.05.004) shares three authors (Solheim, Lundetrae, Uppstad) with the 2024 replication paper and tests an early reading intervention in a group randomized controlled trial, making it a strong candidate for the unnamed original try-out. However, neither the supplied abstract nor the Crossref metadata for 10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.05.004 explicitly names the 'On Track' program or provides the replication's bibliography. The precise unresolved question is whether the unnamed original 'On Track' try-out study retested in 10.1080/19345747.2024.2333734 is identical to shipped row 1566 (Solheim et al., 2018) or refers to a different original report.

decisions.quote: To understand how laypeople define empathy, Hall, Schwartz, and Duong (2021) asked U.S. participants to rate how well items from various empathy measures matched their own definitions. The current paper (N = 549) is a replication of Hall, Schwartz, and Duong (2021, Study 2) using a highly similar study procedure, with a small extension consisting of items from an emotional contagion scale.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent (never previously adjudicated). The candidate target (Hall, Schwartz, and Duong, 2021, Study 2) is already represented by shipped input_row_index 1229 (Hall, Schwartz, & Duong, 2020, 'How do laypeople define empathy?', The Journal of Social Psychology, vol. 161, issue 1, pp. 5-24, doi:10.1080/00224545.2020.1796567). As verified in the Crossref bibliography metadata, the original article by Judith A. Hall, Rachel Schwartz, and Fred Duong was published online in September 2020 (hence year_o='2020' in shipped row 1229) and assigned to volume 161, issue 1 in 2021 (hence the '2021' citation year in the replicating paper's title and abstract). The exact three-author team and study description ('To understand how laypeople define empathy, Hall, Schwartz, and Duong (2021) asked U.S. participants to rate how well items from various empathy measures matched their own definitions') positively establish report equivalence with input_row_index 1229. A fresh literal quote from the primary abstract is supplied in place of the invalid Luna duplicate_quote.

decisions.location: Discussion, paragraph 1; see also Introduction and Methods
decisions.quote: Moreover, the poor phonological decoders with DD not only demonstrated less sensitivity to the FD illusion compared to the typical reading age- and IQ-matched group (supporting Pammer and Wheatley, 2001 ), but also to a reading-level and IQ-matched control group. The latter result excludes that the M-D deficit is simply an effect of DD. This is the first study to show that the M-D deficit in children with DD is present also when compared with younger children with the same reading performance, challenging the idea that the M-D deficit is a simple effect of reading deprivation and not a cause, as recently suggested by Olulade et al. (2013) .
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent (never previously adjudicated). The candidate target Olulade, Napoliello, & Eden (2013, 'Abnormal visual motion processing is not a cause of dyslexia', Neuron, doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2013.05.002) is positively established as background/theoretical context rather than an empirically retested target study, whereas the actual empirical target is already represented by shipped input_row_index 697 (Pammer & Wheatley, 2001, 'Isolating the M(y)-cell response in dyslexia using the spatial frequency doubling illusion', doi:10.1016/s0042-6989(01)00092-x; sibling target_index 0). In the Introduction and Methods, the authors explicitly adopt the spatial frequency-doubling (FD) perimetry task and settings of Pammer and Wheatley (2001) to test magnocellular-dorsal (M-D) sensitivity in Italian dyslexic children with poor phonological decoding versus chronological-age controls (Experiment 1), and then conduct an internal replication of Experiment 1 in a new group of poor phonological decoders while extending the FD illusion paradigm to include a reading-level (RL) control group (Experiment 2, motivated in the Introduction by citing Goswami, 2003, noting that 'The RL children (see Goswami, 2003 ) were never included in previous studies using FD illusion'). Olulade et al. (2013) is never mentioned in Methods or Results, appears in the Introduction only in parenthetical '(e.g., ...)' background lists of controversy/noise-exclusion accounts, and is cited once in the Discussion as a general causal interpretation ('the idea that the M-D deficit is a simple effect of reading deprivation and not a cause, as recently suggested by Olulade et al. (2013)') challenged by the novel RL extension. A fresh literal quote preserving the exact source spacing before the final period is provided.

decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent (never previously adjudicated). In this 1977 Journal of Political Economy paper ('Household Allocation of Time and Religiosity: Replication and Extension'), Ehrenberg uses new survey data from the 1965 National Fertility Survey (over 5,600 females and their spouses, Tables 1 and 2) and the 1969 National Jewish Population Study (2,427 families, Table 3) to re-estimate annual church/synagogue attendance equations specified as similarly as possible to Tables 5 and 6 of Azzi and Ehrenberg (1975, 'Household Allocation of Time and Church Attendance', J.P.E. 83, no. 1: 27-56, explicitly cited in the opening paragraph, footnote 3, and the reference list), finding mixed support in the fertility survey and strong support in the Jewish population survey. The sole shipped row (input_row_index 2254, Long & Settle, 1977, 'Household Allocation of Time and Church Attendance: Some Additional Evidence', J.P.E. 85, no. 2: 409-413, doi:10.1086/260572) is a separate replication paper by different authors published in the same 1977 JPE issue that also tested Azzi and Ehrenberg (1975); Ehrenberg critiques Long and Settle's methodology in footnote 1 to motivate his own replications, but does not re-analyze Long and Settle's data or re-estimate their specific models. Report equivalence does not apply because Long and Settle (1977) and Azzi and Ehrenberg (1975) are distinct works by different author teams.
